### Measurement model {#sec-measurement-model}

Suppose a pupil $p$ is up for an evaluation.
They will receive a provisional advice from their teacher, and a test advice from the test provider $t$.
Both measurements attempt to estimate the common factor: the pupil's suitability for secondary tracks $\theta_p$.
Subscript $p$ marks parameters that vary per pupil, subscript $t$ -- parameters that vary per test.

Since the test is administered by schools, and schools choose their test, pupils taking different tests come from different populations.
We assume that $\theta_p$ is normally distributed within each test population with mean $\mu_t$ and variance $\sigma^2_{\theta, t}$:

$$
\theta_p \mid (\text{pupil }p\text{ takes test }t) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma^2_{\theta, t}).
$$ {#eq-common-factor}

Then we can model the teacher's latent provisional advice $L^*_p$ for pupil $p$ as follows:

$$
L^*_p = \alpha_L \theta_p + \beta_L + \epsilon_{L, p} = \theta_p + \epsilon_{L, p}, \quad \epsilon_{L, p} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_L),
$$ {#eq-teacher}

The latent scale is normalized with respect to the teacher's advice, by setting $\alpha_L = 1$ and $\beta_L = 0$.
Thus, $\theta_p$ is measured in units of the teacher's scale.
In the reference population ($t = \text{ref}$),
we also set the mean of the teacher's judgement to zero, $\mu_{\text{ref}} = 0$, and variance to one:
$\Var(L^*_p | t = \text{ref}) = \sigma^2_{\theta, \text{ref}} + \sigma^2_L = 1$.
These scaling choices are made to fix the origin and unit of the latent scale.
$\epsilon_{L, p}$ is the teacher's error, which can be attributed to the misjudgements about the pupil, as well
as the information that is not visible to the test (e.g., motivation, work ethic, or behaviour).

Now, we model the latent test advice $T^*_p$ as follows:

$$
T^*_p = \alpha_t \theta_p + \beta_t + \epsilon_{T, p}, \quad \epsilon_{T, p} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{T, t}).
$$ {#eq-test}

The loading factor $\alpha_t$ and the intercept $\beta_t$ are specific to the test provider $t$.
$\alpha_t$ encodes the test's sensitivity to the common factor:
a higher $\alpha_t$ distributes the test results more widely for different $\theta$ value (pupils' abilities).
This sensitivity can be affected by factors such as the design, length, and difficulty of the test.
The intercept $\beta_t$ encodes the test's leniency:
a higher $\beta_t$ shifts the test results to a higher track.
The test scale is normalized with respect to the teacher's scale,
by setting $\alpha_{\text{ref}} = 1$ and $\beta_{\text{ref}} = 0$ for the reference test.
The test error $\epsilon_{T, p}$ can be attributed to the test's measurement uncertainty [@cito2026] and
is assumed to be normally distributed.
We set the mean of the error to zero so that every systematic bias is captured by the intercept $\beta_t$,
and we set the variance $\sigma^2_{T, t}$ to be specific to the test provider $t$.

Neither the teacher's advice nor the test result is directly observed;
instead, we observe the provisional advice $L$ and the test result $T$ as ordinal variables.
When $L^*$ falls into the interval between the thresholds of $i$ and $i + 1$, the teacher assigns a provisional advice $i$ to the pupil.
When $T^*$ falls into the interval between the thresholds of $j$ and $j + 1$, the test assigns a test result $j$ to the pupil.

Let $\lambda_1 < \ldots < \lambda_9$ be the thresholds for the teacher's advice
and $\tau_1 < \ldots < \tau_5$ be the thresholds for the test result,
with $\lambda_0 = \tau_0 = -\infty$, $\lambda_{10} = \tau_6 = \infty$.
Then we can write:

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_p = i \Leftrightarrow \lambda_{i} < L^*_p \leq \lambda_{i+1}, \quad &i = 0, \ldots, 9 \\
T_p = j \Leftrightarrow \tau_{j} < T^*_p \leq \tau_{j+1}, \quad &j = 0, \ldots, 5.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-thresholds}

This makes our model a one-factor ($\theta$) measurement model with two congeneric indicators ($L, T$),
with the teacher's advice as the reference indicator.

A pupil is eligible for a higher track if $G(L_p, T_p) > 0$.
Let $\pi \in [0, 1]$ be the compliance -- the probability that a teacher raises the advice when
the test result is higher than the provisional advice.
We can then define $U_p \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$ as an independent uniform draw.
An eligible pupil's advice is raised if $U_p \leq \pi$.
Now, we can define the final advice $F_p$ as follows:

$$
F_p = \begin{cases}
    w_{T_p} \quad &\text{if } G(L_p, T_p) > 0 \text{ and } U_p \leq \pi, \\
    v_{L_p} \quad &\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-final-advice}

@fig-measurement-model shows the structure of the described model.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-measurement-model
%%| fig-cap: "Structure of the measurement model"
flowchart LR
    theta(["`Common factor &nbsp $$\theta_p$$`"])
    lstar(["`Latent provisional advice &nbsp $$L^*_p$$`"])
    l(["`Provisional advice &nbsp $$L_p$$`"])
    tstar(["`Latent test result &nbsp $$T^*_p$$`"])
    t(["`Test result &nbsp $$T_p$$`"])
    gap(["`Advice gap &nbsp $$G(L_p, T_p)$$`"])
    f(["`Final advice &nbsp $$F_p$$`"])

    theta --> lstar
    theta --> tstar
    lstar --> l
    tstar --> t
    l --> gap
    t --> gap
    gap --> f
```

Assumptions made:

- the teacher error variance $\sigma^2_L$ and the provisional advice thresholds are the same for all pupils in every test population,
- the test result thresholds are the same for all tests (CvTE provides a framework for matching the results, see @cvte2026),
- pupils are independent of each other,
- the common factor $\theta$ and the error terms $\epsilon_L$ and $\epsilon_{T, t}$ are all mutually independent,
- the common factor $\theta$ and the error terms $\epsilon_L$ and $\epsilon_{T, t}$ are normally distributed.
